title: Grandmasters are being made younger
p1: Every dot is one of the 1,316 players who became a grandmaster between 2001 and 2025, placed by the year of the title and their age at the time. The dark dots mark the typical age in each five-year spell: 25 at the start of the century, 21 now. Keep an eye on the bottom of the cloud as well – more and more players are getting the title while they're still at school.

title: India: young from the start
p1: India's grandmasters have always been young – the typical one earns the title at 20 – but now there are far more of them: 61 since 2013, against 24 in the twelve years before. Gukesh and Praggnanandhaa both qualified at 12.

title: USA: the biggest change of all
p1: The typical new American grandmaster used to be a seasoned 26-year-old. Since 2013 it has been an 18-year-old, and in 2021 Abhimanyu Mishra became the youngest grandmaster in history, at 12 years and 4 months.

title: Russia: still the biggest factory
p1: No nation has produced more grandmasters since 2001 than Russia – 164 – though far fewer since 2013 than before. Its new grandmasters have got younger too, from a typical age of 24 to 22.

title: China: young, and staying young
p1: China's new grandmasters have typically been just 21 – younger than the world as a whole – and that has held steady for 25 years. Hou Yifan and Wei Yi both earned the title as young teenagers.

title: Ukraine: ahead of its time
p1: Ukraine got there early: Sergey Karjakin became the youngest grandmaster ever in 2002, at 12 years and 7 months. Since 2013 the flow of new Ukrainian grandmasters has slowed, to 23 from 52 in the years before.

title: Germany: later bloomers
p1: German players tend to reach the title later than most – the typical age has stayed around 25. Vincent Keymer, a grandmaster as a teenager, is the exception that may point to the future.

title: The record that keeps falling
p1: The youngest grandmaster on record has gone from 26 to 12 in seventy years. Bobby Fischer's mark stood for 33 years; since 1991 it has been broken seven times. And seven of the ten youngest grandmasters in history qualified in 2018 or later.

title: The elite moves in waves
p1: Each column is the world top 100 in January, split by age – the darker the square, the more players. Follow the dark patch: in the 2000s a wave of twenty-somethings, Carlsen's generation, swept into the elite and then grew older together, pushing the average age up through the 2010s. Since 2022 a new wave has arrived, and the top 10 of January 2026 is the youngest this century.

title: Where the grandmasters are
p1: Grandmasters on each nation's FIDE list every January. Russia still has the most, though its count fell after 2022 as many players switched federation. India's climb is the steepest: five grandmasters in 2001, ninety today.

title: India: from five to ninety
p1: In 2001 India had five grandmasters. Today it has ninety – only Russia, the USA and Germany have more – and the newest of them are among the youngest in the world.

title: USA: more than doubled
p1: The American list has grown from 48 grandmasters to 111: home-grown prodigies, plus strong players who chose to move to the USA.

title: Russia: past its peak
p1: Russia's list peaked at 240 grandmasters in 2021 and 2022. Since then it has fallen to 183, as many Russian players switched federation.

title: China: quiet growth
p1: China's list has grown from 9 grandmasters in 2001 to 54 today – fewer than its rivals, but they include Ding Liren, world champion in 2023.

title: Ukraine: a long plateau
p1: Ukraine doubled its grandmasters in the 2000s, from 37 to 73, then levelled off at 85 to 90.

title: Germany: growing, and greying
p1: Germany's list has doubled to 102 grandmasters, but it is ageing – half the grandmasters on it are now 54 or older.

title: The new 2700s are teenagers
p1: Each line runs from a player's birth to the first year they were rated 2700 or more – the mark of the world's elite. In the 2000s the typical newcomer was in their mid-twenties. Since 2018, eleven players have got there by 20 – five of them still teenagers, Gukesh and Alireza Firouzja at just 17.

title: India's 2700 club
p1: Eight Indian players have reached 2700 for the first time since 2002, six of them since 2018. Gukesh got there at 17, Praggnanandhaa at 19 and Arjun Erigaisi at 20.

title: America's 2700 club
p1: Five Americans have joined the 2700 club since 2018, among them Jeffery Xiong and Hans Niemann at around 20.

title: Russia's 2700 club
p1: Russia has sent more new players past 2700 than any other nation since 2002 – 22 – but only six since 2018, and Andrey Esipenko is the only one to do it by 20.

title: China's 2700 club
p1: China's eight 2700 players include Wei Yi, who got there as a teenager – but none has joined since 2018.

title: Ukraine's 2700 club
p1: Ukraine's 2700 players came early: Ruslan Ponomariov and Sergey Karjakin both did it as teenagers in the 2000s. None has joined since 2018.

title: Germany's 2700 club
p1: Only two Germans have joined since 2002: Arkadij Naiditsch in 2012 and Vincent Keymer in 2024.

title: ENDGAME
p1: So, is chess getting younger? At the top, yes: the newest grandmasters, the newest 2700s and the world champion are younger than ever. But it comes in waves – a generation arrives, stays and gets older together. Magnus Carlsen has topped every January list since 2010 and is now in his mid-thirties, while the players chasing him keep getting younger.
